commenti.body: The Killer character himself must be some kind of millionaire for owning that kind of property and all the gadgets and vehicles he has planted everywhere. So he's in the end a millionaire hired to do the grunt work of a billionaire, dressing as 'working class'. Real life examples of that sort are the talk radio figures who are at least tools to legitimize the interests of capital. The killer is emptied of any qualities but that does not necessarily make him an alienated _worker_ , but a capitalist subject that is indifferent to qualities and only adopts them to pile up more money.

Great analysis, thanks. This is the first reading of the film I’ve seen that really clicks and makes the film more than merely a genre piece or some sort of meta-essay about filmmaking (I don’t see that part at all). Still think it’s mid-level Fincher, but I find myself appreciating it more in hindsight reading stuff like this. It’s a very lean film, very precise, and each character and location serves a purpose, like a cog in a well-oiled machine. The “fun” of the film is in seeing Fassbender’s character upend that machine, even if in a relatively minor way. But his violent quest does expose the hierarchy of capital and its underworld of murder, secrecy, cover-ups and overall transactional view of humanity.

I guess I'm the resident "fuck The Killer" guy on this sub now, so I might as well take a crack at this one. 

So, again, I'm a communist. I think a Marxist reading of this film would fuck if it made any sense. You make a fairly compelling case on a lot of points, and I attempted a reading similar to this as I watched it, but there's 2 pretty big holes that I think invalidate the reading in the end:

1. This reading requires taking almost every aspect of the film as symbolic and allegorical, and you have to ignore some pretty terrible things on the literal level in order to make it work, such as:
   1. The Killer's complete disdain for every human in the film (with 2 exceptions that prove the rule), and his casual and remorseless murder of working class bystanders who did not even wrong him (the sex worker in the beginning, the cab driver, and presumably the cab manager. You could make the case that Delores falls into here too, at minimum her culpability is similar to The Killer himself).
   2. This is kinda an extension of the above, but a critically important aspect of Marxism is solidarity in general, but class solidarity in particular. This is just dead on arrival, the Killer demonstrates absolutely no solidarity to another human being whatsoever, unless you count the extremely meager concession to Delores of not destroying her reputation after murdering her (which you shouldn't). 
2. There's no explaining away the choice to not kill the billionaire. He is a remorseless unflinching murder machine for 90 minutes, and upon being confronted with that thing what represents capitalism itself, as well as the direct cause of his personal grievance, he lets it live and walks away. A Marxist murder machine shoots the billionaire in the dome and walks away, and that's all there is to it. Fundamentally, it casts The Killer as a coward and (not to put too fine a point on it), an irredeemable piece of shit. He knew he could get away with murdering everyone else in his way, but upon being confronted with a risk, and the only thing he actually encountered that might have a chance at actually altering the status quo a little, he walks away.

In the end, I think it's a huge stretch to say that The Killer's actions did anything whatsoever to upend the existing hierarchy. Everything in his world existed because there was a profit incentive for it to exist. He did exactly zero to alter that reality, and along the way he did a bunch of heinous things. 

The conclusion of the film is a shrugging, lazy acceptance of the status quo as inevitable and unchangeable, and in the end, this is the least Marxist part of the entire thing. He demonstrates no class consciousness, and nothing is upended. 

The Killer starts off as a sophomoric rebuke of Marxism, and is capped off by a nihilistic acquiescence to the inevitability of the neoliberal hegemony.

I don’t think he’s a Marxist hero in the way the OP describes.  He’s not that sympathetic a protagonist, so that’s apt anyway.  So while it’s not a straight Marxist film, there are still a lot of themes in the movie that you can read a lot into via class analysis.  

IMO it’s more compelling to read the Killer as an elite worker (eg in tech).  The movie then explores the tension between his budding class consciousness in the face of the callousness of the boss, the self important individualist neoliberal narratives he tells himself, and his desire to just not risk that much when you have the money to be chilling on the beach.  Being in tech during this past year of layoffs, let me tell you, that’s a spot on description of many millionaire Silicon Valley tech workers.
